about: How an animal moves, by taxon (pipeline/locomotion.py resolves a species: every node from kingdom down to the species merges over the one above it, so a value is set once at the widest rank where it holds and overridden only where a narrower group differs; the numbers a species does not give are derived from its body by the allometric rules in locomotion.py, from mass_kg and size in its record). Units: m, m/s, s, rad/s. docs/movement.md explains the principles and which rank each belongs to.

Animalia.note: every animal: muscle shortens, so motion is a pull toward a point; mass sets the tempo (small is quick, large is slow); the body accelerates before it is drawn there (a lag), and nothing moves by itself: a limb or a fin pushes against the world and the body follows

Chordata.note: an axial skeleton: the head leads, the spine bends toward the turn, the tail trails; the body is bilateral and faces where it goes

Mammalia.note: limbs under the body (parasagittal), so the legs swing fore and aft and the gaits are walk, trot (or pace) and gallop, chosen by speed through the Froude number of the hip height (Alexander and Jayes 1983: walk to 0.5, trot to 2.5, gallop beyond); the spine flexes in the gallop; the head stays level over the stride; endotherm, so a sprint is aerobic for seconds to a minute by size
Mammalia.feet: turn by stepping: a standing turn walks in place, the fore feet toward the turn and the hind feet away, planted feet still on the ground

Artiodactyla.note: unguligrade on hooves: a stiff-legged walk, a long trot, a bounding gallop; the alert is a frozen stance, head high

Cervidae.note: the stot (all four feet off together) when alarmed, the white rump flag; a doe and a fawn walk in file

Carnivora.note: digitigrade (cats and dogs) or plantigrade (bears); a flexible spine that lengthens the gallop; the stalk, the rush and the pounce

Canidae.note: the trot is the travelling gait, hours long; the gallop is for the chase; the tail carries the mood. The catch is the mousing pounce: the prey fixed by ear with the head cocked, a frozen braced stance, a high stiff-legged spring onto it with the forelegs straight for the jar, the head down at the forepaws; the first pounce often misses and quick paw strikes follow; the kill is taken in the jaws with a head toss (docs/movement.md The catch)

feed.pose: the kill tossed in the jaws, then the nose down at it

Felidae.note: a crouched stalk, then an explosive short rush of a few seconds and a pounce; a cat does not run far. The catch is the leap and the neck bite: the rush's last bound launches onto the prey's back, the forelegs reaching, the head driven into the nape or throat; over in seconds; then it feeds crouched over the kill, head low (docs/movement.md The catch)

catch.name: the leap and the neck bite

feed.pose: crouched over the kill, head low

Ursidae.note: plantigrade on the whole foot, an amble (a pace: the two legs of a side together) and a bounding run in bursts. The catch (not drawn yet) is the swat: a forepaw blow, then the bite

Rodentia.note: the bound (the fore pair then the hind pair) at every speed above a walk, the sit-up on the haunches to look and to eat, a quick freeze; small, so the tempo is fast and the turns tight

Sciuridae.note: the tail flagged over the back, the bound with a long flight; the tree squirrels climb head-first down

Cricetidae.note: voles and mice: a scurry of quick short bounds close to the ground, runways through the grass

Lagomorpha.note: the half-bound hop: the long hind feet land together ahead of the fore feet; a standing turn pivots on the hind feet with hops of the fore feet; the freeze, then the burst and the zigzag

hop.note: client/src/gait.js hopStep: below shuffle_froude (of the hip height) the shuffle (the fore feet step one after the other, the hind pair hop up behind them); above it the half-bound (the fore feet land one after the other, the hind pair together ahead of them, a flight, the spine flexing and extending); the sit-up, the freeze and the form from the pose; the ears up when alert, laid back in flight or frozen

Lepus.note: the hares: a long lope on long hind legs, and every few bounds of it a higher, longer observation hop to look about

Reptilia.note: ectotherm: speed and endurance with the body's warmth, a sprint of a second or two then a rest; the sprawl

Squamata.note: sprawling limbs out to the side with the body low, and the body undulating side to side with the stride (the lateral wave); a turn is a C-bend of the whole body with the legs stepping round the sprawl; the push-up display

Aves.note: a biped on the ground: walk or hop, the head bobbing to hold the eyes still; the wings for flight: flap to climb, glide to settle, a stoop to dive; the head leads a turn on the neck

dive.note: every bird can close its wings and fall. The speed is a falling body's: weight along the slope against the drag of the tucked body, so it gains g sin(angle) less g (v / terminal)^2 and tends to terminal x sqrt(sin(angle)); terminal = sqrt(2 M g / (rho cd S_b)) with S_b the body's frontal area (pipeline/locomotion.py: Pennycuick's 0.00813 M^0.666 m^2, sea-level air), so it rises with mass^(1/6): a kinglet 31 m/s, a jay 48, a red-tail 74 in a vertical fall nobody has room for. cd 0.37 is the mean measured from the dives of small migrant passerines tracked by radar (Hedenstrom and Liechti 2001, J Exp Biol 204:1167; their range 0.17 to 0.77) and stands for every bird whose own is not measured. angle_deg 64 is the steepest dive track with a source here: a peregrine and a goshawk on tracking radar, 13 to 64 degrees, their fastest 10 s 31 to 39 m/s and about 30 m/s, well under terminal (Alerstam 1987, Ibis 129:267); no group's own steepest angle was found measured, so it stands for the class. A red-tail's 120 mph (54 m/s) and a golden eagle's 150 to 200 mph are repeated without a measurement behind them and are not used. pull_g_at_half_top: the spread wings at full lift slow a 1 kg model falcon at 1.5 g at half its top speed (Tucker 1998, J Exp Biol 201:403), taken as the drag that sheds the dive's speed in the pull-out, as the square of the speed; modelled for a falcon, used for all. What keeps a jay's or a quail's drop short is the height it has, not a number here

Galliformes.note: runners first: a quick walk and a run with the head bobbing, a scratch and peck; flight is a burst flush of a few seconds and a glide downhill; no stoop of their own is recorded and none is given here: the class's fall applies, from the few metres a flush reaches

Passeriformes.note: hop on the ground, perch; flapping flight with glides between (the jays), or the raven's long cruising flight

Corvidae.note: walk as well as hop; the raven soars and tumbles. The catch is the bill stab: small prey (a lizard, a vole, a nestling) killed with repeated hard jabs of the bill at the head and chest until it is still; a jay dives, grabs in the bill and pecks; then it plucks and opens it with the bill (docs/movement.md The catch)

Accipitriformes.note: the soaring hawks: a slow flap, circling on thermals, a stoop

Accipitridae.note: the hawks' catch is the talon strike: from a perch or a stoop the wings fold and it drops, the legs and feet thrown forward at the last moment to grab, the kill by the talons piercing; then it mantles over the kill, wings half spread and drooped round it, head down (docs/movement.md The catch)

catch.name: the talon strike and the mantle

feed.pose: mantling: wings half spread and drooped round the kill, the tail fanned, head down

Falconidae.note: the falcons: the stoop, a long near-vertical dive with the wings closed to a teardrop, the strike in the air or at the ground

dive.note: cd 0.18 is the body drag measured on a peregrine at low speed, with which model falcons of 0.5 to 2 kg top out at 89 to 112 m/s in a vertical dive after about 1200 m (Tucker 1998, J Exp Biol 201:403); a trained 1.02 kg gyrfalcon tracked optically dived at 17 to 62 degrees from up to 500 m (Tucker, Cade and Tucker 1998, J Exp Biol 201:2061; its fastest quoted second hand as about 58 m/s, the paper's own figure not read). angle_deg 87 has no tracked measurement behind it: the vertical stoop is the model's and the field descriptions', the tracked dives stop at 64 degrees; it is this game's limit for a stoop at prey since 2026-11-06

Cathartiformes.note: the vultures: teetering soar with the wings in a dihedral, rarely flapping

Piciformes.note: the woodpeckers: undulating flight (flap, close the wings, fall, flap), cling to the bark, hitch up it

species.note: a species names what no rank above it does: its size and mass (in its record), its own speeds where measured, its displays. Values here override the tree; the rest derive from the body.
